source_blocks.text: Brain-computer interfaces form a separate line of development. They connect signals from a nervous system with external equipment. Neuralink's January 2026 update reported 21 trial participants. Such work may create valuable assistive options. For a sovereignty framework, adoption remains a personal choice. Access to ordinary services, personal AI or civic participation should not depend on accepting an implant.

Unidentified anomalous phenomena, often shortened to UAP, and claims of concealed or non-human technology do not supply a reproducible engineering baseline in the sources reviewed for this paper. They are therefore not assigned computing capacity or deployment dates in the projections. New evidence could change that assessment. The scale established through disclosed spending, equipment and construction is already sufficient to justify serious preparation.
The missing middle for sovereignty

The preceding sections describe systems large enough to shape national choices. Luke Nathan Hayes's proposal, A Fair Go in the Age of Superintelligence, asks what physical and civic capacity people need between their own devices and those vast systems. Its public submission and discussion of possible futures, checked on 5 November 2026, place that question within a broader argument for shared capability and self-determination.

links.text: A Fair Go in the Age of Superintelligence

source_blocks.text: The missing middle in A Fair Go in the Age of Superintelligence is shared local computing infrastructure. Hayes's supplied compute submission, dated 18 August 2026, proposes racks that give communities serious processing capacity they can govern and use. A household computer serves one scale of need; a distant industrial data centre serves another. Locally controlled equipment supplies useful capacity between them, while connecting with larger systems when people choose.

Think of the role of a public library, a workshop at a technical and further education college, or TAFE, and a local emergency-services facility. Each gives people access to equipment, skills or resilience that most households could not efficiently provide alone. A computing facility could offer related benefits: machines, training, practical assistance, secure local storage and continuity during an outside disruption. The exact ownership arrangement would have to be chosen and documented locally.

The physical proposal requires more than a cabinet of expensive chips. Electricity, cooling, communications, trained maintainers, replacement budgets and rules for allocating access all belong in the operating plan. A locally owned machine can still depend on foreign chips or software. Sovereignty grows when those dependencies are understood, several workable options exist and an external service failure does not disable every essential function.

Hayes's 18 August 2026 submission used Australian 6 million dollars per location as an initial planning allowance covering equipment and supporting facilities. At that assumed cost, 100 locations would require Australian 600 million dollars, and 1,000 would require Australian 6 billion. These calculations, made on 5 November 2026 from the submission's allowance, show the order of funding involved. The original worldwide thought experiment applied the same allowance to 44,000 locations, reaching Australian 264 billion dollars. The next useful step is a costed pilot with measured use and operating expenses.

The supplied submission names Dunwich on Minjerribah, also known as North Stradbroke Island, as a possible starting location. That local starting point does not limit the purpose to Redlands. The infrastructure idea concerns personal sovereignty, local data sovereignty, national resilience and self defence. Practical self defence includes protecting records, resisting unauthorised control, maintaining communications and retaining the capacity to operate through disruption.
Individual Auras use that capacity

Aura of Intelligence is the software project at the centre of Hayes's work. The intended arrangement is for people to have individual Auras: personally controlled AI that can learn their authorised context and help them use available tools and computing resources. The Aura of Intelligence public site and Personal Aura page, checked on 5 November 2026, provide entry points. Hayes's design calls for open-source software that people can inspect and modify, personally owned models, and agents that carry out authorised tasks. It has no required dependence on OpenAI or another frontier-model provider. Licences and access to the model files must allow those ownership promises to work in practice.

An individual Aura is closer to a person's chosen assistant and working memory than to the local computer facility itself. It could help organise a project, find relevant information, prepare a document or use additional local processing when a task exceeds the person's own device. The individual remains in charge of what it may remember, which tools it may use and when it should stop.

Keeping information, retrieving it and changing a model are separate operations. A personal archive can hold documents and memories. Search can bring selected material into a current task. Further training can change how the model responds. A meaningful ownership arrangement must make these choices visible rather than silently mixing them together. It also needs practical export, backup and migration so the person can move their records and working setup.

A digital twin is a digital representation used to describe or simulate something in the world. A farm twin might represent paddocks, rainfall and equipment; a personal representation might hold someone's preferences and chosen history. Its usefulness depends on accuracy, correction and consent. The person represented must be able to reject an inference, change a record or stop participating. Hayes's supplied whole-of-life Aura material places personal continuity and practical support within this software ambition.

Consider an illustrative community project, constructed for this paper on 5 November 2026. A resident on Minjerribah wants to help a local food garden plan water use. Their Aura helps assemble the questions and keeps their private calendar and personal notes on their chosen equipment. A community-owned rack performs a heavier simulation using permitted weather, soil and infrastructure data. The rack provides the machinery. The individual Aura helps its owner use it.
The Web3 sensorium connects what people choose to share

The Web3 sensorium is the proposed intermediary layer between individual Auras, devices, shared computing and wider information. Sensorium refers to the ways a system gathers and makes sense of observations. Web3, in this proposal, concerns distributed control and verifiable cooperation between independently operated systems. Hayes's supplied c-hour plan, dated 23 September 2026, explicitly describes participation without requiring cryptocurrency purchases or expertise.

Think of it as a combination of a switchboard and a map room. It helps the right information reach the right place, while preserving who supplied it, when it was measured and what permissions apply. The public Web3 Sensorium page, dated 9 May 2026 and checked on 5 November, describes a research direction involving local control, shared models, evidence and public debate. It remains a proposed architecture whose protections have to be implemented and tested.

source_blocks.text: In the garden example, the sensorium could connect an authorised soil reading with a public weather forecast and the shared water model. It would not need the resident's private messages or complete personal history. If a result were shared publicly, people should be able to inspect the source, date and assumptions. The Minjerribah Living Twin public project, checked on 5 November 2026, provides a related place-based entry point for exploring digital representations.

This intermediary layer has an important trust problem to solve. Copies already disclosed cannot always be recalled by pressing a revoke button. Consent therefore needs to govern collection and disclosure in advance, with limited retention, clear recipients and enforceable obligations. A promise of personal control becomes credible through demonstrated behaviour: what leaves the device, who can decrypt it, what happens offline and whether the person can leave with usable records.
Purple Party for Australia provides the proposed civic layer

P4A stands for Purple Party for Australia. Its public civic workbench, checked on 5 November 2026, describes a proposed movement and drafting project. In Hayes's architecture, it aims to provide the civic layer: a place for people to understand the rules that govern them, examine evidence, develop changes and build support through democratic processes.

source_blocks.text: Its scope extends beyond one council. A resident may first encounter a problem through a local road, housing issue or service, while the power to change it sits with a state parliament or the Commonwealth. P4A's intended role is to help people follow that chain, understand what a proposal would do and work towards an informed, winnable pathway to change. Other countries would need processes fitted to their own institutions.

An Australian analogy is a community meeting that has access to a good library, clear maps and time to rehearse the consequences of a proposal. People still disagree and decide. The tools help them see which authority is responsible, which claims have evidence and what trade-offs they are being asked to accept. The Australian Law and Personal Relevance public project, checked on 5 November 2026, is a related entry point into that learning work.

source_blocks.text: A constitutional referendum has a particular threshold. The Australian Electoral Commission's explanation checked on 5 November 2026 states that a change requires a national majority of voters and a majority in at least four of the six states. A simulation or local vote does not enact the change. P4A's proposed contribution is the groundwork: understanding the law, testing possible wording, listening to objections and building the public support needed for the formal process.

Returning to the garden example, the sensorium might show that an apparent water problem also involves a planning rule or public infrastructure decision. Individual Auras could help participants understand the material. The shared rack could run agreed scenarios. P4A could support the civic discussion about a proposed change. The participants, through the appropriate democratic institutions, would retain the decision. This is how the physical, personal, intermediary and civic parts fit together.
A reason to keep participating

Infrastructure becomes socially useful when people can build worthwhile lives around it. Hayes's c-hour, or community-hour, proposal addresses reciprocity: recognising contributions to other people and the community without assigning those hours a monetary equivalent. The C Hours introduction, checked on 5 November 2026, sits alongside the supplied 23 September 2026 planning document. Individuals and communities decide what they are willing to offer to people earning c-hours. In the wider braided-economy proposal, monetary activity and voluntary reciprocity can coexist without requiring every contribution to become a price.

The garden provides a simple illustration. Someone contributes time to watering or teaching. A participating group might choose to offer access to a workshop, an outing or another activity. The offer is voluntary and locally decided. The hour is a record of contribution, with no fixed conversion into dollars. Whether the arrangement builds trust depends on fair access, sensible verification and the freedom not to participate.

The Global Association for Joyful Responsible Abundance on Earth, shortened to GAJRA Earth, is Hayes's proposed voluntary association network. Its public project page, identified in the supplied material and checked on 5 November 2026, provides a starting point. Joy asks whether life is worth participating in. Responsibility asks what the activity does to other people and the living world. Abundance asks whether capability can expand access and possibility. Keeping all three together provides a practical test of what the technology is for.

Culture belongs in that account. Hayes's A Protopian Gambit music project, checked on 5 November 2026, expresses a wager on building a future people want to keep improving. Shared worlds, music, humour and art can give technological participation a human purpose. A decentralised network, with independently controlled worlds connected by choice, would be judged by whether people can create, cooperate, disagree and leave while keeping meaningful control of their own lives.

That right to leave is central to the whole architecture. People should be able to disconnect, decline a model's advice, refuse an implant and keep private parts of life outside a shared system. An individual Aura, a local rack, a sensorium connection or a civic organisation earns trust by making those choices workable.
What would make sovereignty real

The immediate task is to turn the proposed local capacity into something people can examine and use. A pilot should demonstrate useful work, an affordable operating model and continuity through an outside outage. It should show a person moving their Aura and records, a community deciding who administers the equipment, and an independent reviewer checking what privileged operators can do. These are recommendations from this paper, dated 5 November 2026.

Ownership must include practical authority. A community facility needs clear rules for selecting maintainers, approving sensitive changes, resolving disputes and paying for replacement equipment. No single administrator should silently acquire control over every personal record or connected machine. The ability to pause a service locally, preserve evidence and restore a known working version is as important as headline processing speed.

There are existing public-capacity programmes to learn from. The US National Science Foundation's 2026 account of its National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource reported support for hundreds of teams and thousands of students. The European Commission's AI factories programme checked on 5 November 2026 links shared computing with assistance for users. The UK Government's 2025 Compute Roadmap committed public investment towards 2030. These programmes have different purposes and governance arrangements, but show that access to substantial computing can be organised beyond a direct personal subscription to a single commercial model provider.

source_blocks.text: Australia can participate in the global build-out while developing its own capacity to choose. The major corporations supply equipment, research and services of enormous potential value. Their military links, concentrated voting power and control over critical dependencies make scrutiny essential. Shared local racks, individually controlled software, carefully governed connections and informed civic participation address different parts of that problem.

The central choice is whether people gain capability alongside the machines. The industrial scale is already immense, and its consequences reach well beyond a better chatbot. Building useful, accountable capacity close to people is a practical way to make personal sovereignty, local resilience and national self defence part of the same technological future.
How the projections were calculated

This section records the assumptions and calculations prepared on 5 November 2026. It separates terrestrial electricity, orbital power, comparable processor capacity and robot production. Company targets provide dated reference points; interpolations, growth rates and service lives are this paper's assumptions. The scenarios test possible expansion mechanisms without assigning probabilities. Mining, refining, materials innovation and AI-assisted improvement can change the growth rates. They are treated as conditions to measure, rather than permanent limits or automatic breakthroughs.
Terrestrial electricity

The terrestrial reference starts at 485 terawatt-hours in 2025 from the International Energy Agency's 16 April 2026 report. From 2025 to 2030, the low case grows by 10 per cent annually, the reference case by about 14.392 per cent and the high case by 20 per cent. The reference reaches 950 terawatt-hours in 2030. From 2030 to 2036, the assumed rates are 3, 5 and 12 per cent respectively. This includes power supplied to terrestrial data centres through grids or local generation. It excludes the additional orbital fleet modelled below.

For 2027, the low, central and high electricity results are 587, 635 and 698 terawatt-hours. For 2028, they are 646, 726 and 838. For 2029, they are 710, 830 and 1,006. For 2031, they are 805, 998 and 1,352. For 2036, they are 933, 1,273 and 2,382. Results are rounded to whole terawatt-hours.

Every Australian comparison divides the relevant result by 286.8 terawatt-hours, Australia's calendar-2025 generation in the 2026 government release. Continuous-power examples multiply gigawatts by 8,760 hours and divide by 1,000 to obtain terawatt-hours in a 365-day year. They assume continuous use at the stated power. Electricity generation, equipment rating and delivered computing work remain distinct quantities.
Comparable terrestrial AI processing capacity

The starting point is 31.6 million H100-equivalents from Epoch AI's 16 September 2026 research. Epoch estimated 20.3 million at the end of 2025, then extrapolated to September 2026; the latter was not a direct September census. H100 is the reference NVIDIA accelerator used to compare different equipment. Epoch's methodology checked on 5 November 2026 explains how equipment is compared and the allowance for deployment delays. This paper's model estimates theoretical processing capacity. Useful output also depends on memory, communications, software and the work being performed.

From the 2026 baseline to 2031, the terrestrial low case assumes powered capacity grows 10 per cent annually and processing per unit of power improves 15 per cent. The reference assumptions are 20 and 30 per cent; the high assumptions are 25 and 40 per cent. Multiplying these factors gives annual processing multipliers of 1.265, 1.56 and 1.75. These are assumptions made on 5 November 2026, informed by scaling research including Epoch AI and the Electric Power Research Institute's 11 August 2025 study. They already allow compounded growth; they are not a complete model of what future SI could improve.

From 2031 to 2036, the illustrative terrestrial cases use powered-capacity growth of 3, 8 and 15 per cent annually, with hardware efficiency gains of 10, 20 and 30 per cent. The resulting multipliers are 1.133, 1.296 and 1.495. This selected slowdown is a scenario assumption, not a claim that continued faster expansion is impossible. AI-assisted chip design, new processes and greater production could justify a different path. Software improvements to useful work per calculation should be reported separately from physical processor capacity.

The terrestrial processing and electricity series remain separate sensitivity calculations for different equipment populations. They are not a single solved energy balance. Combining them into one physical fleet forecast would require measured processor performance per watt, the equipment mix and utilisation. The new orbital calculations address power and deployment explicitly without inventing that missing processor conversion.

The terrestrial results, in millions of H100-equivalents, are 40, 49 and 55 for 2027; 51, 77 and 97 for 2028; 64, 120 and 169 for 2029; 102, 292 and 519 for 2031; and 191, 1,067 and 3,873 for 2036. Each sequence gives low, reference and high. The orbital power cases are not converted to H100-equivalents because their future processor mix and measured performance are not established. A combined processor total would need those measurements and must count each physical machine only once.
How factory capacity enters the scenarios

The factory review checks major publicly disclosed projects against the five horizons. It includes advanced processor fabs, memory and storage plants, packaging, and factories making supporting electronics. Semiconductor companies' investment totals are not converted directly into computing capacity. A new building may still need equipment; installed equipment may still need qualification; initial output can take time to reach the planned rate.

To calculate processing capacity from the factories, start with wafers processed each month, allow for the production ramp, and count the usable chips per wafer. Then establish how many are allocated to AI products. Matching memory and packaging must be available before completed systems can be shipped, connected and powered. The running fleet accumulates those additions and loses equipment through retirement. This resembles estimating the grain available in a town: the silo's handling capacity, this year's deliveries and the stock already stored are three different figures.

SEMI's third-quarter 2026 public summary supports multiplying 100 by 1.08 annually after 2026, through 2029 only. This review used the public summary, not the full paid database. Company checks cover major disclosed projects rather than every plant. Faster processing growth additionally requires better chips, improved production yields, more output allocated to AI and sustained deployment. Wafer-capacity growth alone cannot validate the central processing scenario.

The calculations avoid counting the same capacity twice. The named projects sit within the broader industry expansion, so their totals are not added on top of SEMI's aggregate. Plants already producing before the baseline contribute only subsequent growth. An acquisition changes ownership without itself creating more worldwide production. Processor, memory and packaging capacity describe complementary stages and cannot be summed as equivalent processors. Missing Chinese production details remain an explicit uncertainty.

The International Energy Agency's 16 April 2026 report already considered semiconductor and memory supply constraints in its energy outlook. That does not establish that its April projection included each later factory announcement. The new construction evidence makes the industrial pipeline more visible, especially in 2027 to 2029, without resolving undisclosed AI allocations, usable output, retirement rates or the power available to operate the resulting equipment. The retained numerical cases should therefore be read as conditional scenarios, not forecasts validated by every fab in construction.
Orbital power and accumulated capacity

The orbital ambition case uses year-end annual commissioning rates of one gigawatt in 2027, ten in 2028 and one hundred in 2029, following the scale in the 8 June 2026 SpaceX technical talk. This paper selects 200 in 2030 and 300 in 2031, then holds the annual rate at 300 through 2036. The 300-gigawatt choice represents one numerical interpretation of the several-hundred-gigawatt scale in Musk's 5 February 2026 interview. The intermediate years and the continuation after 2031 are assumptions dated 5 November 2026, rather than company guidance.

Commissioning rates increase smoothly between those year-end points. The incremental fleet starts from zero at the end of 2026; that modelling convention excludes existing demonstrations rather than claiming they do not exist. For example, a rate rising from zero to one gigawatt per year over 2027 delivers half a gigawatt during that year. A rate rising from one to ten during 2028 delivers another 5.5 gigawatts, taking the end-year fleet to six. An annual deployment rate is therefore kept distinct from the installed fleet.

Each commissioned unit is assumed to carry adequate generation and heat-rejection equipment for its rated computing load. The model assumes average operation at 80 per cent of that rating and replacement after five years. Both are this paper's 5 November assumptions, not measurements of a future fleet. The average operating fraction covers the difference between rated and realised electrical load, including outages and derating. It does not apply an Earth-grid availability constraint. Replacement removes old equipment from the stock before the next year's total is calculated.

Energy equals the average surviving rated fleet during the year, multiplied by 80 per cent and 8,760 hours. Converting gigawatt-hours to terawatt-hours requires dividing by 1,000. The ambition case's orbital energy is approximately 1.2 terawatt-hours in 2027, 17.5 in 2028, 182 in 2029, 2,296 in 2031 and 10,395 in 2036. The smaller case uses one-tenth of every commissioning rate and therefore one-tenth of these energy figures. Both scenarios are conditional on successful manufacturing and deployment; a multi-year delay would shift the trajectory.

The reported combined totals add orbital consumption to the unrounded terrestrial reference. They describe electrical energy used by the two computing systems, not new demand on terrestrial grids. Orbital power refers to the computing load; spacecraft support equipment, manufacturing, mining, robot charging and launch energy are outside that comparison. Adding the two paths assumes extra orbital production and demand alongside terrestrial construction. If the same chips or customer workloads move from land to orbit, the terrestrial path must be reduced accordingly. The chip supply cannot be counted twice.

Using the earlier assumption of 100 kilowatts of rated compute per tonne, 100 gigawatts of annual additions requires approximately one million tonnes of complete computing payloads delivered annually. At 300 gigawatts, it requires three million tonnes. With 100 tonnes per dedicated flight, those are 10,000 and 30,000 successful computing-payload flights respectively. These are 5 November 2026 requirements of the hypothesis, not a forecast that all launches carry computers. A verified doubling of usable compute per delivered tonne would halve the mass and flight requirements.

Operating fraction and service life have large effects. For a fleet with the same deployment history, 100 per cent average operation would produce 25 per cent more computing energy than the 80 per cent assumption. Once a constant 300-gigawatt annual deployment programme matures, three-year replacements sustain about 900 gigawatts of stock and five-year replacements sustain about 1,500. These sensitivities identify useful engineering measurements instead of treating the Sun's energy supply as the limiting quantity.
Humanoid production and useful robot fleets

The established industrial-robot reference remains the International Federation of Robotics' 24 September 2026 forecast: 655,000 annual installations in 2026 and 806,000 in 2029. A constant-growth interpolation gives about 702,000 in 2027 and 752,000 in 2028. These figures cover that established market. The new humanoid hypotheses below address a separate emerging production system and do not use the industrial forecast as a ceiling.

The delayed adoption hypothesis assumes worldwide humanoid production of 100,000 in 2027, growing 50 per cent annually through 2031 and 25 per cent thereafter. The factory expansion hypothesis starts at 500,000, doubles annually through 2031 and then grows 50 per cent annually through 2036. The accelerated hypothesis starts at one million, multiplies production by 2.5 annually through 2031 and then by 1.6 annually through 2036. All starting values and multipliers are assumptions selected on 5 November 2026. They represent increasingly successful commercialisation and industrial improvement, rather than measured orders or confidence intervals.

The starting assumptions span partial realisation through rapid realisation of the disclosed manufacturing programmes. The first million-unit Tesla line is a useful scale reference, with several competing manufacturers contributing globally. Continued growth requires replication of productive lines, expansion of component supply and useful deployments that support reinvestment. The later growth reductions are selected scenarios, not mandatory laws. Faster, slower or interrupted paths remain possible. A single early factory's rapid improvement does not establish the same growth rate for every supplier indefinitely.

Annual production is calculated by repeatedly multiplying the previous year's output by the applicable growth factor. The five forecast years give 100,000, 150,000, 225,000, 506,250 and about 1.54 million in the delayed case. The factory expansion case gives 500,000, one million, two million, eight million and 60.75 million. The accelerated case gives one million, 2.5 million, 6.25 million, 39.06 million and 409.6 million. These calculations explicitly include exponential growth over each period.

For fleet calculations, completed robots are assumed to enter service during the production year and remain for five years. At the end of 2036, the model therefore retains production from 2032 through 2036, giving approximately 5.2 million, 158.3 million and 988.1 million robots. Older machines are retired. These are surviving units under the assumptions, not human-worker equivalents. Useful labour depends on availability, productive hours, task capability and the amount of human support required. Those measures also determine how much robot deployment can accelerate mining and manufacturing.
Testing the feedback hypothesis

The production paths must be checked against their changing physical requirements. Annual material demand equals units produced multiplied by material per unit, adjusted for manufacturing losses and recycled supply. For orbital systems, useful power per tonne links the capacity scenario to spacecraft mass and launches. For robots, accepted output per line and the number of productive lines link annual production to factories. These relationships make the growth hypotheses testable.

The main indicators are completed output, yield, machine availability, useful work per hour, the time required to open another production line, refined material delivered and material required per unit. For AI-assisted discovery, the relevant sequence is predicted candidate, reproducible measurement, qualified component and manufacturing-scale adoption. Improvements at any stage can accelerate the loop; a sustained shortfall changes the achievable rate. Shared chip and material supplies must be allocated across programmes before combined scenarios can be treated as a consistent world forecast.

The stronger hypothesis gains support if AI and robots measurably shorten factory expansion, improve recovery and refining, reduce material requirements or increase useful computing per watt and per tonne. It weakens if those improvements fail to reach production while costs, failures or delivery delays rise. Uncertainty about this feedback does not make exponential expansion impossible. It makes the feedback strength and the time needed to realise it central research questions. No extra unspecified SI multiplier is added on top of the already compounded numerical cases.
Reading the evidence

Financial filings provide dated disclosures of spending, commitments and voting rights. Company announcements provide reported operations and management targets. Government publications establish the permissions, plans or figures they describe. Independent studies bring their own coverage and estimation methods. A filing's publication date and the period measured are both retained where available. Where a public page provides no reliable publication day, this paper gives the available month or year and the date checked.

The local sovereignty sections draw on Hayes's supplied documents and the public project pages linked in the text. The supplied compute submission is dated 18 August 2026; the supplied c-hour planning edition is dated 23 September 2026. The individual Aura and layer definitions also incorporate Hayes's explicit clarifications in this discussion. Proposed capabilities are described as design intentions. An accessible public page demonstrates published material, rather than independent proof that every described system is deployed.

chapters.title: When intelligence becomes infrastructure
chapters.summary: AI matters beyond the screen when the software, electricity, machines and authority to act become part of the same system.
chapters.markdown:
An AI assistant can help write a letter. Give the same software access to your calendar, files and booking service, and it can begin carrying out parts of the work. Connect it to a warehouse, a truck or a laboratory, and its instructions can change what happens in the physical world. The question becomes who may give those instructions, what the system is allowed to do, and how the people affected can challenge a mistake.

Artificial intelligence, or AI, is software that learns patterns and uses them to generate answers, make predictions or guide actions. A model is the learned software itself. An agent combines a model with access to tools and an arrangement for pursuing a task. Its practical agency comes from the actions that arrangement permits. Reading a document, sending a message and changing a machine each carry a different level of responsibility.

Superintelligence, shortened to SI, describes the ambition for systems that exceed human capability across many important activities. There is no agreed instrument that can tell everyone exactly when that threshold has been crossed. People also disagree about when it might arrive and how controllable it would be. The reviewed sovereignty paper therefore starts with things that can be examined today. It follows the money, equipment, electricity, industrial production and authority being assembled around that ambition. Its evidence cutoff is 5 November 2026.

The physical side matters. Compute means the processing work a computer can do. Chips perform calculations, memory feeds them information, storage keeps records, and networks connect the parts. A rack holds a connected set of equipment. A data centre contains many machines with the power, cooling and communications needed to run them. The cloud is computing equipment you reach through a network, operated by a supplier somewhere else.

Renting that equipment can be useful. It lets a small organisation access facilities it could never sensibly build on its own. The relationship changes when it depends on that supplier for its records, daily procedures, staff expertise and ability to keep working. A price increase, policy change, outage or withdrawal can then affect the organisation's freedom to act. Sovereignty is meaningful authority over your own affairs, whether you are a person, community or country.

Consider a mine buying its communications, dispatch software, battery storage and automated machinery from a closely connected group of suppliers. Every service may offer real benefits. Together, they also determine whether the mine can function and who can change its behaviour. Hospitals, farms and public agencies face related choices. Physical location is one part of the arrangement. Access rights, software updates, usable copies of records and workable alternatives matter as well.

Electricity helps make the scale visible. Power measures the rate at which electricity is used, while energy measures how much is used over time. The paper uses Australia's calendar-2025 generation of 286.8 terawatt-hours as a fixed measuring stick, drawing on the Australian Government's 2026 statistics release. A fleet drawing 13 gigawatts continuously for a year would use about 40 per cent of that amount. At 100 gigawatts it would use roughly three such Australian totals. These comparisons describe an assumed continuous electrical load, rather than intelligence or useful work.

The central possibility is that the industries reinforce one another. Better computing can improve designs and factory operations. Robots can help make and maintain more equipment. Improvements in mining, materials and energy can support further expansion. A machine becomes more consequential when it helps enlarge the production system that makes the next machine.

That possibility can produce worthwhile gains in medicine, safety, creative work and disaster preparation. It can also concentrate influence over the systems people need to live. The practical issue is whether human capability and authority grow alongside machine capability. Following who supplies the equipment, who funds it and who holds the deciding votes makes that question much more concrete.

chapters.title: Who owns the machinery and the decisions
chapters.summary: The race combines model developers, cloud companies, factories, investors and governments. Their figures measure different things, and their ownership structures differ.
chapters.markdown:
The businesses in the AI race occupy different positions. Some build models, some rent out computing, some make processors, and some own several parts of the chain. A cloud provider can also be an investor in a model company and a competitor selling its own AI. Understanding these relationships is more useful than imagining a single firm doing everything on its own.

The reviewed paper keeps several kinds of financial claim apart. Capital spending buys or builds equipment and facilities. A purchase commitment sets out future obligations. A financing announcement describes investment arrangements. A valuation is what investors think a company is worth. A contract ceiling is the maximum that can be ordered under an agreement. Adding all those headlines together would count different things, sometimes counting the same infrastructure more than once. Corporate amounts in this chapter are US dollars.

OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, illustrates the connections. The paper records its March 2026 announcement of US$122 billion in committed funding and its April statement that it had secured more than 10 gigawatts of infrastructure capacity. Secured capacity can include equipment and buildings still to be delivered. Its agreements connect it with NVIDIA, Broadcom, Amazon, Oracle and other participants. A single supply arrangement can appear in announcements from several of them.

The paper describes OpenAI's formal control through the OpenAI Foundation, using its structure page checked on 5 November 2026. It separately records chief executive Sam Altman's personal investments. Those interests can raise questions about conflicts where businesses deal with one another, while formal authority still needs to be traced through the actual boards, ownership rights and agreements.

Anthropic, the developer of Claude, presents another structure. Its 2 November 2026 filing disclosed about US$895.4 billion of computing and infrastructure commitments, with obligations reaching as far as 2045. About US$447.5 billion fell before the end of 2030. That long schedule matters when interpreting the headline. At the paper's cutoff, Anthropic was private with an offering in preparation. Its proposed founder voting arrangements and the Long-Term Benefit Trust's board appointment rights sat alongside substantial commitments to commercial suppliers.

Publicly traded companies can also concentrate decisions. The paper records combined voting power of 52.7 per cent for Alphabet founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin in the relevant 2026 disclosure. A Meta disclosure put Mark Zuckerberg's voting power at 60.6 per cent against a 13.4 per cent economic interest. Different share classes let people hold a relatively small share of the financial interest and a much larger share of the votes. The rights attached to ownership therefore matter as much as the number of outside shareholders.

The machinery has its own chain of dependence. A semiconductor fabrication plant, usually called a fab, makes circuits on wafers. The chips then need memory, packaging, connections and suitable systems around them. The industry association SEMI projected equipment spending for 300-millimetre wafer factories to rise from US$149 billion in 2026 to US$227 billion in 2029. Its public outlook supported roughly 8 per cent annual growth in installed capacity from 2027 through 2029. On that basis, an index of 100 in 2026 becomes about 126 in 2029.

Construction, installed equipment and useful output occur at different stages. A factory may have a building before it has its tools. It may make initial wafers before it reaches reliable production. Processors can wait for memory or packaging, then wait again for power and commissioning. The paper follows those stages across TSMC, Intel, Samsung, Micron and other suppliers rather than converting construction spending straight into working AI.

China is building across this chain too. Its September 2026 national plan targeted 9,800 exaFLOPS of intelligent computing by 2030, compared with 1,882 reported for March 2026 on that plan's measurement basis. An exaFLOP means a billion billion arithmetic operations a second. The accuracy used in a calculation, the hardware counted and whether a figure describes theoretical or delivered performance all affect comparisons. That national total cannot simply be placed beside an estimate based on imported US-designed processors.

Huawei, Alibaba, Tencent, state telecommunications groups and Chinese chip and memory manufacturers have different roles and owners. Their programmes add domestic production and commercial deployment to national policy. For Australia, the question is how to benefit from both international systems while retaining skills, records and operating choices it can control locally. Several suppliers help. Practical authority also needs people who understand the machinery and can keep essential work going.

chapters.title: How computing robots and space could accelerate one another
chapters.summary: Orbital power, reusable transport, factories, robotics and materials discovery form a possible feedback loop. The paper turns that possibility into requirements people can examine.
chapters.markdown:
SpaceX and Tesla offer the paper's clearest example of an attempt to join several industries. Their associated programmes reach from processors, batteries and AI to satellites, reusable rockets, vehicles and humanoid robots. The important relationship is between those capabilities. Improvements in one part could make the others cheaper, faster or easier to expand.

The paper records SpaceX's October 2026 results as reporting 1.7 gigawatts of installed rated capacity in its intelligence business at the end of September. Management targeted 2.5 to 3 gigawatts by December and about another 10 during 2027. Those are dated reported results and management targets, with delivery still to be judged. The Terafab plan extended the ambition to chip production, with an eventual manufacturing goal equivalent to one terawatt of new power-rated computing equipment a year.

That last phrase describes annual output. It is the pace at which machinery would be added. A stock of installed equipment builds as successive additions enter service and reduces as old equipment retires. Keeping the production rate separate from the operating fleet is essential throughout the paper.

Orbit offers a further route. Computing spacecraft carry processors, solar arrays, communications and equipment for releasing heat. In a suitable orbit, solar power can be available with far less interruption from night and weather. The task becomes making and deploying the complete spacecraft, with adequate power and heat rejection for the computing load. Its electricity comes with it, so adding that orbital fleet need not wait for a new connection to a power grid on Earth.

The transport requirement is substantial. Using the paper's stated engineering assumption of 100 kilowatts of rated compute per tonne delivered, adding 100 gigawatts in a year requires one million tonnes of computing payload. At 100 tonnes per flight, that is 10,000 successful dedicated payload flights, averaging about 27 a day. These are calculated requirements of the ambition. They include neither spare capacity for failed launches nor all replacement needs.

Permissions and delivery must catch up with that scale. The paper distinguishes an application for up to one million satellites from an operating constellation. It also distinguishes proposed launch rates under environmental review from authorised flights. A working spacecraft is one test. A repeated service whose full costs, replacement schedule and customer performance are competitive is a larger one. Communications networks from Amazon and Blue Origin, Google's Project Suncatcher and Chinese demonstrations show several organisations pursuing parts of this opportunity.

Robots could help accelerate production on Earth. An industrial robot might be a fixed factory arm. A humanoid has a more human-shaped body, while drones move through air, land or water. The paper records about five million established industrial robots worldwide in a September 2026 industry release. It follows emerging humanoid programmes separately, including Tesla, Figure, Hyundai, Unitree and AGIBOT. Designed factory capacity, machines actually produced and useful machines working for customers each need their own count.

The strongest humanoid scenario in the paper reaches annual production of 409.6 million machines in 2036 and a surviving fleet of about 988 million under its five-year service-life assumption. That is a conditional calculation. At the scale of a proposed ten-million-unit annual production line, 410 million machines would need roughly 41 fully productive equivalents worldwide. At an illustrative 60 kilograms per robot, the annual output would embody about 24.6 million tonnes of finished machines. Those requirements help people test what such a claim entails.

Materials and manufacturing can change the requirements. AI can help improve recovery from processed ore, suggest alternative materials or improve a design. Google DeepMind's GNoME announcement reported millions of candidate crystal structures. A candidate still has to be made, measured, incorporated into a qualified component and produced reliably at scale. Robotic laboratories can shorten parts of that journey by preparing and testing the next experiment.

The feedback hypothesis gains strength when improvements reach production. Useful measures include output per line, the time to open another factory, material per machine, useful computing per watt and computing per tonne delivered to orbit. An improvement in one stage can expand what another can do. Repeated evidence of those improvements would support faster growth. The paper preserves the possibility of a much larger industrial system while giving its expansion concrete tests.

chapters.title: Keeping authority when software can act
chapters.summary: The ability to act through tools and machines raises practical questions about permission, updates, procurement, local control and the right to challenge a decision.
chapters.markdown:
A navigation tool can suggest a route. A dispatch system can allocate the route to a vehicle. An autonomous vehicle can then begin driving it. Each step transfers more practical responsibility to software and the people operating it. The useful question is what authority has been granted, who can change it, and what happens when someone needs the system to stop.

Autonomy describes how much sensing, planning and action a machine can perform without a person directing every step. The surrounding arrangement still has people who select the task, supply access, maintain the equipment and accept responsibility. More capable software can handle a wider range of circumstances, but capability alone does not establish a proper right to act.

The stakes are already visible in military procurement. The paper follows Anduril's autonomous equipment and its Lattice coordination software, Palantir's information systems and the communications and launch services supplied by other firms. US contracts cited in the paper include ceilings of US$20 billion for an Anduril enterprise agreement and US$10 billion for a Palantir agreement. A ceiling permits orders up to a maximum. Actual orders determine what has been bought.

Australia is participating in these systems. A September 2025 government announcement set out an A$1.7 billion, five-year Ghost Shark contract with Anduril Australia for autonomous undersea vehicles, maintenance and further development. An October 2026 announcement described payloads for carrying supplies, deploying sea mines and releasing aerial vehicles. The published account establishes the announced capability and programme, while operational approvals and all targeting arrangements are not fully disclosed.

Civilian systems carry a related form of power. The reviewed paper records Palantir contracts connected with Australian Defence, financial intelligence and state intelligence systems. For several Commonwealth contract values, the review could access public mirrors of AusTender notices and retained the official links. Those figures therefore keep that access limitation and their stated contract periods. They describe recorded purchases, rather than a complete account of government use.

A person can decide which personal assistant to use. They generally have much less choice over the software a public agency uses to handle their information. A credible system needs ways to challenge an error, understand who can see the record and limit reuse. Hosting a machine in Australia can help with particular risks, while authority over its software, administrator access and future updates needs its own account.

Updates are especially consequential when one change can reach many organisations. Microsoft's account of the July 2024 CrowdStrike incident estimated that a faulty security update affected 8.5 million Windows devices. It was an outage caused through a trusted delivery channel. The paper uses that event to show how quickly a common failure can spread. Connecting physical action or weapons to similarly concentrated channels increases the importance of independent controls.

Those controls can be described in everyday terms. One role approves a sensitive change and another carries it out. A staged update lets operators inspect a small deployment before extending it. A local team can isolate an unsafe command, preserve the record and restore a known working version. An independent reviewer can examine what administrators are able to do. Contracts need to cover these behaviours during an outage or emergency as well as ordinary service.

The paper treats concentrated update authority as a risk to design for. A claim about a particular person being able to redirect a fleet would require evidence about that person's actual access. Ownership, credentials, communications and operational command have specific meanings. Careful scrutiny follows the authority that the evidence establishes.

The same discipline belongs in a personal Aura. Recording information, retrieving it for a task, training a model and publishing a result are separate choices. An assistant might prepare a document while waiting for permission to send it. A person should be able to correct its account, decline its advice, move usable records and stop a connection. In the wider system, sovereignty grows when those freedoms are supported by dependable equipment, understandable agreements and people who can enforce them.

chapters.title: Planning for five very different horizons
chapters.summary: The paper tests conditional paths to 2027, 2028, 2029, 2031 and 2036. Its figures make assumptions visible and identify the delivery evidence to watch.
chapters.markdown:
Planning around powerful AI requires a way to think beyond the next product announcement. The reviewed paper uses five horizons measured from 5 November 2026. It combines announced industrial milestones with its own explicit calculations. These are conditional scenarios, with no probabilities assigned. The fastest case is one demanding possibility to examine, and circumstances could produce a faster, slower or interrupted path.

Three different quantities are tracked. Terrestrial electricity is the energy used by data centres on Earth. Terrestrial processing capacity is compared using NVIDIA H100-equivalents, a way of putting different equipment on a common performance basis. Orbital capacity is tracked through rated power, deployment and energy, because the future mix of processors is unknown. Energy use and H100-equivalents describe equipment and operation. Neither measures intelligence directly.

The terrestrial electricity reference follows the IEA's April 2026 path from 485 terawatt-hours in 2025 to 950 in 2030. The paper then assumes 5 per cent annual growth through 2036. Separate low and high paths test different rates. Its processing calculation starts from an estimated 31.6 million H100-equivalents for September 2026, derived from Epoch AI research. Growth in powered capacity and improvements in processing per unit of power compound together. The electricity and processing calculations cover different equipment populations and remain separate sensitivity models.

The orbital ambition case begins with annual commissioning rates rising to one gigawatt by the end of 2027, ten by the end of 2028 and one hundred by the end of 2029. The paper selects rates of 200 in 2030 and 300 in 2031, then holds the latter through 2036. Those later selections are its assumptions, informed by the scale in dated company discussions. Rates rise gradually during each year. A rate reaching one gigawatt a year in December therefore adds half a gigawatt over that first year.

**2027 tests delivery.** The reference terrestrial energy figure is about 635 terawatt-hours, with processing around 1.6 times the September 2026 baseline. The orbital ambition case adds about 1.2 terawatt-hours during the year. The evidence to watch is complete equipment entering useful service, including promised computer facilities, first orbital computing flights and the initial output of new chip and memory plants. The three humanoid cases start with worldwide production of 100,000, 500,000 or one million machines.

**2028 tests manufacturing.** Terrestrial reference electricity reaches about 726 terawatt-hours. The orbital ambition case reaches six gigawatts of installed fleet capacity and adds about 17.5 terawatt-hours of computing energy. Chip-factory, packaging and satellite programmes have important milestones in this period. A building opening late in the year may make most of its contribution later. Humanoid production reaches 150,000, one million or 2.5 million in the three cases.

**2029 tests combination.** Terrestrial reference electricity reaches about 830 terawatt-hours, while the orbital ambition case uses another 182. Their combined figure is about 1,013 terawatt-hours. The relevant questions concern whole services customers can use and maintain. In the manufacturing outlook, the wafer-capacity index reaches approximately 126 against 100 in 2026. The humanoid hypotheses reach annual output of 225,000, two million or 6.25 million machines.

**2031 tests accumulated dependence.** The terrestrial reference is about 998 terawatt-hours. Combined with the orbital ambition case, it reaches roughly 3,294 terawatt-hours. Annual humanoid production reaches about half a million, eight million or 39 million. More of an organisation's records, training and procedures may by then sit within a connected supplier system. Arrangements for moving data and maintaining local operation become harder to add once all of those dependencies are established.

**2036 tests the consequences of compounding.** The terrestrial reference reaches about 1,273 terawatt-hours. The combined total is about 2,313 with the smaller orbital case or 11,668 with the orbital ambition case. The orbital component carries its own generation and places no equivalent load on Earth's grid. The humanoid hypotheses give surviving fleets of about 5.2 million, 158 million or 988 million, assuming five-year service lives. Useful labour still depends on reliability, tasks, operating hours and human support.

The orbital calculations assume average operation at 80 per cent of rated computing power and replacement after five years. They also assume orbital equipment is additional to the terrestrial programme. Shifting the same chips or workloads into orbit would require reducing the Earth-based path. Future quantum systems, materials discoveries and manufacturing improvements could change these trajectories when they demonstrate useful performance.

These assumptions make the scenarios open to correction. A reader can watch completed output, production yields, useful work, replacement rates and expansion time. The point of the horizons is to make decisions while options remain open and to revise the plan as the physical evidence arrives.

sections.title: What could be established by 2036
sections.html:
2031 tests accumulated dependence. The terrestrial reference is about 998 terawatt-hours. Combined with the orbital ambition case, it reaches roughly 3,294 terawatt-hours. Annual humanoid production reaches about half a million, eight million or 39 million. More of an organisation's records, training and procedures may by then sit within a connected supplier system. Arrangements for moving data and maintaining local operation become harder to add once all of those dependencies are established. 2036 tests the consequences of compounding. The terrestrial reference reaches about 1,273 terawatt-hours. The combined total is about 2,313 with the smaller orbital case or 11,668 with the orbital ambition case. The orbital component carries its own generation and places no equivalent load on Earth's grid. The humanoid hypotheses give surviving fleets of about 5.2 million, 158 million or 988 million, assuming five-year service lives. sections.html:
The orbital calculations assume average operation at 80 per cent of rated computing power and replacement after five years. They also assume orbital equipment is additional to the terrestrial programme. Shifting the same chips or workloads into orbit would require reducing the Earth-based path. Future quantum systems, materials discoveries and manufacturing improvements could change these trajectories when they demonstrate useful performance. chapters.title: Making sovereignty something people can use
chapters.summary: Shared local equipment, personal Auras, carefully governed connections and civic practice address different parts of the same question about who gets to act.
chapters.markdown:
A resident wants to help a community garden plan its water use. Their personal notes include a calendar, the people they have spoken with and a few ideas they are still unsure about. The project also needs weather records, soil measurements and a model of the water system. That heavier work could use shared equipment without requiring everyone involved to buy an expensive computer or hand over their whole personal history.

The reviewed paper uses this illustrative garden project to explain the **missing middle**. A phone or household computer serves one level of need. A distant data centre serves another. Shared local equipment can supply serious computing between them, with trained people, useful services and rules the community can examine. The facility can connect to larger systems when that is useful and keep selected local functions available when an outside connection fails.

The supplied compute proposal used A$6 million per location as a planning allowance for equipment and supporting facilities. At that allowance, 100 locations amount to A$600 million and 1,000 to A$6 billion. The worldwide thought experiment of 44,000 locations comes to A$264 billion. These figures express the scale of the proposal. A working deployment also needs site-specific costs, electricity, cooling, communications, maintenance, future replacement and people who can make the equipment useful.

Ownership is expressed through those arrangements. A community needs to know who may administer its equipment, who can approve a sensitive change and what happens when it chooses a different service. It needs a way to resolve disputes and pay for the next hardware generation. Owning the cabinet while losing access to its data, maintenance or essential software would leave major decisions elsewhere. Practical sovereignty joins the asset with the skills, permissions and options needed to use it.

An individual **Aura** would help its owner work with that capacity. In the garden example, it could organise questions and bring back the reasons for earlier choices. The person decides what it may retain, retrieve or use in further model training. Heavier processing can run on a local rack using only the information authorised for that job. Software people can inspect and models they can use under appropriate licences give the ownership promise practical meaning.

The proposed **Web3 sensorium** connects observations, models and systems operated by different people. Here, Web3 concerns distributed control and verifiable cooperation. A soil reading can retain its source, time and permission while being compared with a weather forecast. If a model result is published, other people should be able to inspect its assumptions. Participation in the proposed network does not require buying cryptocurrency. Agreements still need to explain what happens to a copy once it has been released.

A public question may then emerge. The water plan could depend on a planning rule or an infrastructure decision. **P4A, the Purple Party for Australia**, is the proposed civic workbench for following that chain. Participants can identify the responsible authority, examine alternatives, listen to objections and prepare a proposal for the relevant process. A simulation helps people understand consequences. Formal legal and democratic procedures determine how a change is enacted.

People also need reasons and opportunities to keep participating. A C-Hour records one verified hour of voluntary contribution. Communities choose what recognition or reciprocal opportunities to offer, with no fixed dollar conversion. Paid work, investment and equipment expenses retain their own accounts. A garden project can therefore recognise someone's time while also showing what it cost and what changed.

**GAJRA Earth**, the proposed Global Association for Joyful Responsible Abundance on Earth, connects this local capability to relationships across borders. People define worthwhile lives in their own contexts, share learning and choose work they can do together. Joy gives participation a purpose, responsibility carries the consequences, and abundance asks whether useful capability becomes more widely available.

The reviewed paper recommends demonstrating these freedoms in practice. A person moves an Aura and usable records to another system. A community chooses its maintainer and survives an outside outage. An independent reviewer checks privileged access. National sovereignty becomes more tangible when people can exercise those choices in ordinary life.
